name: Foundations
title: Charge, current, voltage and Ohm's law
intro: Electronics starts with a few measurable quantities: charge, current, voltage, resistance and power. These lessons build those ideas with concrete numbers, then contrast AC and DC and cover the safety habits that keep beginners alive. You do not need calculus — arithmetic and careful units are enough.

lessons.title: Electric charge
lessons.summary: Electrons, coulombs, and why charge is conserved.

sections.p: Electric charge is a property of matter. Electrons carry a negative charge; protons carry a positive charge of equal size. The SI unit is the coulomb (C). One electron has about −1.6 × 10−19 C, so one coulomb is roughly 6.25 × 1018 electrons.

Charge is conserved: it can move from place to place, but it is not created or destroyed in ordinary circuits. When a capacitor "charges", charge separates onto its plates; the total charge of the closed system stays the same.

Static cling is charge sitting on an insulator. In a wire, charge is free to move. Electronics mostly cares about moving charge — that motion is current — but static charge still matters for ESD damage to chips.
One ampere-hour is 3600 C. A phone battery around 3000 mAh stores about 10 800 C of separable charge at its terminals — a tiny mass of electrons, but a useful electrical packet.

practice.why: Charge is measured in coulombs. Amperes are charge per second.

lessons.title: Electric current
lessons.summary: Amperes, direction of flow, and typical sizes.

sections.p: Current is the rate of charge flow. One ampere (A) means one coulomb passes a point each second: I = Q / t. A milliampere (mA) is 0.001 A; a microampere (µA) is 0.000001 A.

Schematics draw current from the positive terminal through the load back to the negative terminal. Electrons in metal drift the other way. Datasheets and Ohm's law use conventional current — stay consistent.
An LED indicator might draw 5–20 mA. USB charging at 1 A is a thousand milliamps. A car starter can pull hundreds of amps briefly. A microcontroller GPIO often sources or sinks only a few milliamps.

In a single loop with no branches, the same current flows through every series element. Current is not "used up" by a resistor; the resistor drops voltage while the same amperes continue around the loop.

lessons.title: Voltage (potential difference)
lessons.summary: Volts as energy per charge, and common supply levels.

sections.p: Voltage is electric potential difference: energy available per unit charge. One volt (V) means one joule per coulomb: V = W / Q. A voltage at a point always implies a reference — often circuit ground.
Think of voltage as pressure difference and current as flow rate. High pressure with a closed valve means high voltage and nearly zero current.
Logic boards often use 3.3 V or 5 V. AA alkaline cells start near 1.5 V. A car battery is nominally 12 V. Mains is about 120 V or 230 V AC — treat mains as lethal.
DC has a defined + and −. Reverse a polarized capacitor or many ICs and you can destroy them. On a meter, red on the more positive node gives a positive reading.

lessons.title: Resistance
lessons.summary: Ohms, conductors, insulators, and what resistors do.

sections.p: Resistance opposes current. The unit is the ohm (Ω). A resistor is built to a chosen resistance. For many materials at fixed temperature, voltage and current stay proportional.
Copper has very low resistance for short wires. Glass and most plastics are insulators. A short is an unintended low-resistance path; an open is a broken path.
Thin long wire has more resistance than thick short wire. At high current, even a fraction of an ohm drops voltage and heats up.
1 kΩ = 1000 Ω. 1 MΩ = 1 000 000 Ω. A pull-up might be 10 kΩ; an LED series resistor on 5 V might be a few hundred ohms.

lessons.title: Ohm's law
lessons.summary: V = I R with worked numbers.

sections.p: Ohm's law for a resistor is V = I R, also I = V / R and R = V / I. V is the voltage across the resistor, I the current through it, R its resistance.
A red LED drops about 2.0 V when lit, from a 5.0 V supply. The series resistor must drop 3.0 V. For 10 mA: R = 3.0 / 0.010 = 300 Ω. A standard 330 Ω part is common.
Ideal diodes, LEDs and transistors are not linear resistors. Size the resistor around them with Ohm's law; do not treat the LED itself as a fixed R for all voltages.
12 V across 2.2 kΩ gives I = 12 / 2200 ≈ 5.45 mA. A wildly different meter reading suggests a parallel path or wrong part.

sections.code:
V = I * R
I = V / R
R = V / I

lessons.title: Power and energy
lessons.summary: Watts, P = V I, and heating.

sections.p: Power is the rate of energy use. One watt (W) is one joule per second. In DC circuits, P = V I. For a resistor: P = I² R or P = V² / R. Energy E = P × t.
A common through-hole resistor is rated 1/4 W (0.25 W). At 5 V across 100 Ω, I = 50 mA and P = 0.25 W — at the limit, so pick higher wattage or larger R for comfort.
In a resistor, electrical energy becomes heat. In a motor, much becomes mechanical work plus heat. In an LED, some becomes light; most still becomes heat.
A 3.7 V, 2000 mAh lithium cell stores roughly 3.7 × 2.0 = 7.4 Wh (order of magnitude; usable energy depends on discharge limits).

sections.code:
P = V * I
P = I^2 * R
P = V^2 / R

lessons.title: AC versus DC
lessons.summary: Steady polarity vs alternating, and why both exist.

sections.p: DC keeps the same polarity: batteries, USB rails, most logic supplies. AC reverses polarity over time. Mains is AC at 50 Hz or 60 Hz depending on region.
Transformers need changing magnetic fields, so AC made long-distance voltage conversion practical. Household outlets remain AC even though modern DC links exist.
AC voltage is often quoted as RMS. About 120 V RMS has peak near 170 V. Do not treat RMS as the peak when rating capacitors on the AC side.
Power supplies turn AC into DC with diodes, capacitors and regulators. A phone brick's USB cable carries DC even though the wall side is AC.
Never probe mains casually. Capacitors on the AC side can stay charged after unplugging. Prefer batteries, USB power banks, or current-limited lab supplies.

lessons.title: Measuring with a multimeter
lessons.summary: Voltage, current and resistance the safe way.

sections.p: A digital multimeter (DMM) measures voltage, current and resistance. Wrong jack or mode can blow a fuse — or worse on mains. Start on a battery-powered circuit.
Select V DC. Put probes in parallel with the part. You do not open the circuit to measure voltage.
Put the meter in series. Move the red lead to the current jack if required. Start on a high range. Never put current-mode probes across a supply like a voltmeter.
Measure resistance with power off. Continuity beep finds low-resistance paths — also power off. Charged capacitors confuse ohm readings.

lessons.title: Safety basics
lessons.summary: Mains, heat, batteries, and eye protection.

sections.p: Safety first. Low-voltage battery and USB projects are the right place to learn. Mains can kill. Even low voltage can start fires with a shorted lithium pack.
Do not open mains-powered equipment unless trained. Capacitors can hold charge after unplugging. Prefer isolated lab supplies and sealed commercial USB adapters.
Soldering irons are typically 300–400 °C. Use a stand, never catch a falling iron, and work with ventilation. See the soldering course for joint and fume detail.
Wear eye protection when clipping leads or desoldering. Do not puncture or short Li-ion cells; charge only with proper chargers. A puffed pack is scrap.
A bench supply limited to 100–200 mA turns many wiring mistakes into teachable moments instead of smoked traces.
